newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentine unions, gov't to set labor talks agenda.
newsitem.headline: Argentine unions, gov't to set labor talks agenda.

text.p: Argentine unions will meet Thursday with government officials to hammer out an agenda for talks on labor reform plans, CGT union federation head Rodolfo Daer said Monday.
"This time around we will set up an agenda for future meetings in which businessmen will participate," Daer told the state-run Telam news agency.
The CGT and the government resumed labor reform talks last week after President Carlos Menem tried and failed to introduce the changes, adamantly opposed by unions, by decree.

The CGT staged a 24-hour general strike in December to fight the decrees, which would give the government powers to revoke collective pay deals, let firms negotiate with unions on a company-by-company and not an industry-wide basis and let smaller firms bypass national unions in wage talks.
Reform plans also include replacing redundancy pay with unemployment insurance and ending union control of healthcare.

But Menem's attempts to introduce reforms by decree were blocked by two judges. The government immediately invited unions back to the negotiating table and urged businessmen to take a more active role.
The Argentine Industrial Union (UIA) said Monday it was losing patience with attempts to make labor laws more flexible and complained the government was showing signs of caving in to CGT demands.
"There can be no political excuses for not carrying out these reforms," wrote UIA chief Jorge Blanco Villegas in the daily Clarin.
"Over the last few days, from some sectors of the government and the union movement there has begun to arise an anti-business line of argument," he wrote.
Also writing in Clarin Monday, Menem argued Argentina needed his decrees to compete and to help businesses reduce unemployment, standing at a near-record 17.3 percent.

"They have to be aided by legislation which is realistic and which fits in with the real world, which takes account of the needs of those who want to work and of those who want to give work," he wrote.
